Larval development in Potamilus purpuratus begins with the release of glochidia, which are brooded within the marsupial demibranchs of the female until they are expelled into the water column. At the moment of birth, newly released glochidia possess a diminutive shell length of only 0.02 centimeters [Lb = 0.02 centimeters], a size that reflects their obligate parasitic reliance on a suitable fish host for continued development. Following a brief period of host attachment and metamorphosis, the juvenile bivalve ultimately undergoes settlement onto the substrate, at which point the prodissoconch has reached a shell length of approximately 0.03 centimeters . This transition from a parasitic larva to a benthic juvenile represents a critical bottleneck in the species' early life history, as successful settlement depends upon encountering appropriate substratum conditions. The entire process from glochidial release to the completion of metamorphosis is strongly influenced by ambient thermal conditions, with warmer temperatures generally accelerating the rate of development.

As individuals progress through their juvenile phase and approach sexual maturation, shell growth proceeds steadily until the onset of reproductive capability is attained. Field surveys and mark-recapture studies have indicated that Potamilus purpuratus reaches puberty, defined by the development of functional gonadal tissue capable of gamete production, at a shell length of roughly 9 centimeters [Lp = roughly 9 centimeters]. This size threshold corresponds to an age of approximately 20 years, based on incremental growth line analyses conducted on specimens collected from populations in the lower Mississippi River drainage. The ultimate shell length that individuals can achieve under favorable conditions has been documented at 15 centimeters [Li = 15 centimeters], a size that represents the asymptotic maximum observed in long-lived populations occupying stable habitats. Attaining this maximum dimension requires several decades of uninterrupted growth, and is often only realized by individuals that escape predation and disease throughout their extended lives.

Adult body composition in well-developed specimens of Potamilus purpuratus has been characterized through dry mass determinations performed on individuals collected from productive riverine habitats. The ultimate dry weight, representing the maximum somatic mass achieved after accounting for shell material and water content, has been estimated at 121.5 grams [Wwi = 121.5 grams]. This value was derived through size-corrected comparisons with related unionid species and reflects the substantial metabolic investment required to build and maintain such a large bivalve body over a long lifespan. In contrast to many short-lived freshwater mussels that allocate resources rapidly toward reproduction, this species displays a more gradual pattern of mass accumulation, consistent with its iteroparous life history and extended reproductive window. Populations inhabiting nutrient-poor streams may exhibit lower mean dry weights, but the maximum recorded figure provides a useful benchmark for comparing somatic condition across different river systems and geological settings.

Reproductive output in Potamilus purpuratus has been quantified through direct counts of glochidia released by gravid females of known body size. For an individual with a shell length of 10.45 centimeters, the daily reproductive rate, maintained under stable water temperatures of 17 °C [T = 17 °C], reaches approximately 1,144 glochidia per day [Ri = approximately 1,144 glochidia per day]. This substantial fecundity is necessary to offset the high mortality experienced during the parasitic larval stage, where only a tiny fraction of released glochidia successfully encyst on a compatible host fish and complete metamorphosis. The reproductive rate is temperature-dependent, with cooler conditions slowing the release of brooded larvae and warmer conditions accelerating the process. Field observations suggest that females in southern populations, where growing seasons are longer, may sustain elevated reproductive rates over extended periods, thereby maximizing lifetime offspring production despite the inherent uncertainties of host encounter rates.

Longevity constitutes one of the most remarkable aspects of the life history of Potamilus purpuratus, with maximum lifespan in natural populations commonly exceeding nine decades. Under controlled thermal conditions at 17 °C [T = 17 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan from laboratory-maintained individuals extends to 11 years [am = 11 years], though this figure likely underestimates the true potential of wild specimens due to the artificial constraints of captivity. In contrast, field studies conducted by Bauer in 1987 documented that ages of 93 years are typical for undisturbed natural populations. The age at birth, representing the duration of embryonic development within the female's marsupial gills before glochidial release, has been measured at 10 days [ab = 10 days] when water temperatures reach 16 °C [T = 16 °C]. This brief incubation period is comparable to that of other congeners and reflects the relatively simple glochidial morphology that characterizes this lineage.
